He also wanted to know which aspects of the stories had fewest 33 __________, as he believed these aspects would be the most important ones. Contrary to other beliefs, he found that some 34 __________ that were included in a story tended to change over time, and that the middle of a story seemed no more important than the other parts. He was also surprised that parts of a story which seemed to provide some sort of 35 __________ were unimportant. The aspect that he found most important in a story’s survival was 36 __________.

questions.prompt: On leaving school, Moore did what his father wanted him to do.
questions.evidence: After leaving school, Moore hoped to become a sculptor, but instead he complied with his father’s wish that he train as a schoolteacher.
synonymSubstitutions: did what his father wanted = complied with his father’s wish
On leaving school = After leaving school
questions.distractors: Moore personally hoped to become a sculptor, but the word ‘instead’ confirms that he followed his father’s wish, so FALSE is excluded; the action is explicitly stated, so NOT GIVEN is excluded.

questions.prompt: Moore began studying sculpture in his first term at the Leeds School of Art.
questions.evidence: Although he wanted to study sculpture, no teacher was appointed until his second year.
synonymSubstitutions: began studying sculpture = a sculpture teacher was appointed
first term conflicts with until his second year
questions.distractors: His first year is mentioned, but he spent most of it drawing; the explicit ‘until his second year’ contradicts ‘in his first term’, so TRUE and NOT GIVEN are excluded.

questions.prompt: When Moore started at the Royal College of Art, its reputation for teaching sculpture was excellent.
questions.evidence: In September 1921, he moved to London and began three years of advanced study in sculpture.
questions.evidenceLocation: paragraph 2; the passage states his study but gives no evaluation of the College’s reputation
synonymSubstitutions: started at the Royal College of Art = moved to London and began three years of advanced study
excellent reputation has no stated equivalent
questions.distractors: The passage says he studied there and later mentions its instruction, but never rates its reputation; absence of that comparison rules out TRUE and FALSE.

questions.prompt: Moore became aware of ancient sculpture as a result of visiting London museums.
questions.evidence: During these visits, he discovered the power and beauty of ancient Egyptian and African sculpture.
synonymSubstitutions: became aware of = discovered
as a result of visiting London museums = During these visits
questions.distractors: The preceding sentence identifies the London museums, especially the British Museum; the discovery is explicitly tied to those visits, so FALSE and NOT GIVEN are excluded.

questions.prompt: The Trocadero Museum’s Mayan sculpture attracted a lot of public interest.
questions.evidence: When he visited the Trocadero Museum in Paris, he was impressed by a cast of a Mayan* sculpture of the rain spirit.
questions.evidenceLocation: paragraph 4; only Moore’s reaction is stated, not the public’s
synonymSubstitutions: attracted Moore’s interest = he was impressed
public interest has no stated equivalent
questions.distractors: Moore’s fascination cannot be generalised to public interest. The passage neither confirms nor denies the public response, excluding TRUE and FALSE.

questions.prompt: Moore thought the Mayan sculpture was similar in certain respects to other stone sculptures.
questions.evidence: Moore became fascinated with this stone sculpture, which he thought had a power and originality that no other stone sculpture possessed.
synonymSubstitutions: similar to other stone sculptures conflicts with originality
in certain respects conflicts with a power ... that no other ... possessed
questions.distractors: The passage explicitly presents the sculpture as unique rather than similar, so TRUE and NOT GIVEN are excluded.

questions.prompt: The artists who belonged to Unit One wanted to make modern art and architecture more popular.
questions.evidence: The aim of the group was to convince the English public of the merits of the emerging international movement in modern art and architecture.
synonymSubstitutions: wanted = the aim
make ... more popular = convince the English public of the merits
questions.distractors: ‘The group’ refers directly to Unit One, and its stated aim supports the claim, excluding FALSE and NOT GIVEN.

questions.prompt: Moore is urged to offer his 8 __________ and leave the Royal College
questions.evidence: There were calls for his resignation from the Royal College
synonymSubstitutions: is urged = there were calls for
offer his = his
questions.distractors: ‘contract’ appears later, but it expired rather than being offered; ‘resignation’ is the exact one-word noun required after ‘his’.

questions.prompt: Moore turns to drawing because 9 __________ for sculpting are not readily available
questions.evidence: A shortage of materials forced him to focus on drawing.
synonymSubstitutions: not readily available = a shortage of
turns to drawing = forced him to focus on drawing
questions.distractors: ‘shortage’ expresses the condition but does not name what is unavailable; ‘materials’ is the plural noun that fits both meaning and grammar within the one-word limit.

questions.prompt: While visiting his hometown, Moore does some drawings of 10 __________
questions.evidence: In 1942, he returned to Castleford to make a series of sketches of the miners who worked there.
synonymSubstitutions: visiting his hometown = returned to Castleford
drawings = sketches
questions.distractors: ‘Londoners’ were subjects of earlier sketches in London, not during the return to his hometown; ‘miners’ is the exact one-word answer.

questions.prompt: Moore is employed to produce a sculpture of a 11 __________
questions.evidence: In 1944, Harlow, a town near London, offered Moore a commission for a sculpture depicting a family.
synonymSubstitutions: is employed to produce = offered ... a commission for
of a = depicting a
questions.distractors: ‘Harlow’ is the commissioning town, not the subject; ‘family’ is the exact one-word object of the sculpture.

questions.prompt: 12 __________ start to buy Moore’s work
questions.evidence: In this way, Moore’s work became available to collectors all over the world.
synonymSubstitutions: start to buy = became available to
Moore’s work = Moore’s work
questions.distractors: ‘copies’ describes the editions, while ‘collectors’ names the people who could acquire the work and fits the plural subject before ‘start’.

questions.prompt: Moore’s increased 13 __________ makes it possible for him to do more ambitious sculptures
questions.evidence: The boost to his income enabled him to take on ambitious projects and start working on the scale he felt his sculpture demanded.
synonymSubstitutions: increased = the boost to
makes it possible = enabled him
do more ambitious sculptures = take on ambitious projects
questions.distractors: ‘scale’ relates to the size of later work but was not what increased to enable it; ‘income’ is the exact one-word cause.

questions.prompt: Section A
questions.evidence: Travelling around Thailand in the 1990s ... Two decades later Janssen developed that basic idea ... into a portable device
synonymSubstitutions: initial inspiration ↔ basic idea he saw in Southeast Asia
new product ↔ developed ... into a portable device
distractors: vi is tempting because the final phrase mentions purifying water, but the paragraph’s full progression is from the Thai solar-heating inspiration to Janssen’s later device.
ii, vii and ix describe benefits, production problems or reception that paragraph A never discusses.

questions.prompt: Section B
questions.evidence: can take water from different places, such as the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain, and purify it for human consumption
synonymSubstitutions: a range of sources ↔ the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain
cleaning water ↔ purify it for human consumption
distractors: x is supported by statistics only in paragraph D, not by this description of water sources.
v focuses on the device’s differentiating selling point, which is paragraph C.

questions.prompt: Section C
questions.evidence: Its main selling point is that unlike standard desalination techniques, it doesn’t require a generated power supply: just sunlight.
synonymSubstitutions: what makes the device different ↔ main selling point
alternatives ↔ standard desalination techniques
distractors: ii might seem possible because portability is useful, but the paragraph explicitly labels sunlight-only operation as the main selling point.
vii is wrong because the paragraph explains operation, not production difficulties.

questions.prompt: Section D
questions.evidence: at least two-thirds of the world’s population lives with severe water scarcity ... by 2030 half of the world’s population will be living with water stress
synonymSubstitutions: the number of people ↔ two-thirds ... half of the world’s population
water shortages ↔ severe water scarcity / water stress
distractors: vii is tempting because expensive plants and maintenance are mentioned, but these are access barriers rather than difficulties making the Desolenator.
iv concerns user groups and markets in paragraph E.

questions.prompt: Section E
questions.evidence: aimed at a wide variety of users – from homeowners in the developing world ... to people living off the grid ... niche markets ... camping, on boats, or for the military
synonymSubstitutions: range of potential customers ↔ wide variety of users
customers ↔ homeowners / people living off the grid / niche markets
distractors: i is about raising production finance, whereas microfinance here is a way for customers to pay.
ix is unsupported: field tests and expected deployment do not describe a warm welcome.

questions.prompt: Section F
questions.evidence: We are a venture with a social mission ... to be a viable company there is a bottom line to keep in mind
synonymSubstitutions: profit not the primary goal ↔ a venture with a social mission
profit ↔ bottom line
distractors: i is wrong because the paragraph discusses selling prices and mission, not obtaining production funding.
iv belongs to paragraph E’s discussion of user groups.

questions.prompt: Section G
questions.evidence: It has raised £340,000 in funding so far. Within two years ... the company aims to be selling 1,000 units a month
synonymSubstitutions: getting the finance ↔ raised £340,000 in funding
production ↔ aims to be selling 1,000 units a month
distractors: iv is wrong because named sales regions are not a description of customer types.
ix would require evidence of a positive reception, which paragraph G does not give.

questions.prompt: The device can be used in different locations, as it has 21 __________.
questions.evidence: It measures 120 cm by 90 cm, and is easy to transport, thanks to its two wheels.
synonymSubstitutions: used in different locations ↔ easy to transport
has ↔ thanks to its two
distractors: transport describes the benefit but cannot follow ‘it has’; the required noun copied from the passage is ‘wheels’.
pipe and tubes are components, but they do not explain mobility.

questions.prompt: Water is fed into a pipe, and a 22 __________ of water flows over a solar panel.
questions.evidence: Water enters through a pipe, and flows as a thin film between a sheet of double glazing and the surface of a solar panel
synonymSubstitutions: is fed into ↔ enters through
over a solar panel ↔ between ... and the surface of a solar panel
distractors: thin is only an adjective and cannot fill the noun slot after ‘a’.
sheet refers to double glazing, whereas the flowing layer of water is a film.

questions.prompt: Any particles in the water are caught in a 23 __________.
questions.evidence: The device has a very simple filter to trap particles
synonymSubstitutions: are caught ↔ trap
particles in the water ↔ particles
distractors: boiler converts water to steam but is not stated to trap particles.
pipe carries water into the device; it does not catch particles.

questions.prompt: The purified water comes out through one tube, and all types of 24 __________ come out through another.
questions.evidence: There are two tubes for liquid coming out: one for the waste – salt from seawater, fluoride, etc. – and another for the distilled water.
synonymSubstitutions: purified water ↔ distilled water
all types of ↔ salt from seawater, fluoride, etc.
distractors: salt and fluoride are examples, but neither alone covers ‘all types of’ material from the other tube.
liquid is too general and does not contrast with purified water.

questions.prompt: A screen displays the 25 __________ of the device
questions.evidence: The performance of the unit is shown on an LCD screen
synonymSubstitutions: displays ↔ is shown
device ↔ unit
distractors: information is transmitted by the screen but the specific thing displayed is the device’s performance.
LCD identifies the type of screen and cannot fill the object after ‘displays the’.

questions.prompt: the company so that they know when the Desolenator requires 26 __________.
questions.evidence: transmitted to the company which provides servicing when necessary
synonymSubstitutions: requires ↔ when necessary
they know when ↔ transmitted to the company
distractors: maintenance appears later in paragraph D in a discussion of conventional desalination plants, not what the Desolenator’s company provides.
performance is the preceding blank and is the data transmitted, not the service required.

questions.prompt: In fairy tales, details of the plot
questions.evidence: People of every culture tell each other fairy tales but the same story often takes a variety of forms in different parts of the world.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph A, opening sentence; physical page 68.

distractors.A: Biological methods provide insights into development, not the details themselves.
distractors.B: The passage rejects useful/cautionary content as the chief reason for survival.
distractors.D: No analysed plot is said to contain animals transforming into humans.
distractors.E: Oral origin describes the corpus of 58 stories, not plot details.
distractors.F: The absence of a factual basis concerns speculative social theories, not plot details.

synonymSubstitutions: details of the plot ↔ the same story ... takes a variety of forms
global ↔ different parts of the world
considerable variation ↔ a variety of forms

questions.prompt: Tehrani rejects the idea that the useful lessons for life in fairy tales
questions.evidence: Yet in his analysis such elements were just as flexible as seemingly trivial details.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph G, third sentence; physical page 69. The preceding sentence identifies these as survival-relevant cautionary elements.

distractors.A: This ending belongs to insights into fairy-tale development (Q30).
distractors.C: Global variation describes plot forms, not useful lessons.
distractors.D: Transformation into humans is never stated.
distractors.E: Being spoken rather than written describes the source traditions.
distractors.F: Unsupported theories are the various academic theories, not the lessons themselves.

synonymSubstitutions: useful lessons for life ↔ cautionary elements / information relevant to survival
are the reason for their survival ↔ important enough to be reproduced from generation to generation

questions.prompt: Various theories about the social significance of fairy tales
questions.evidence: That hasn’t stopped anthropologists, folklorists* and other academics devising theories to explain the importance of fairy tales in human society.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph B, fifth sentence; physical page 68. The preceding quotation stresses the huge knowledge gap.

distractors.A: Biological methods are Tehrani’s way to test ideas, not an ending for the theories themselves.
distractors.B: Theories are not stated to be the reason the tales survive.
distractors.C: Variation applies to plot versions around the world.
distractors.E: Oral tradition describes the 58 source stories.

synonymSubstitutions: social significance ↔ importance ... in human society
have been developed ↔ devising theories
without factual basis ↔ huge gap in our knowledge

questions.prompt: Insights into the development of fairy tales
questions.evidence: Tehrani has used the same approach to compare related versions of fairy tales to discover how they have evolved and which elements have survived longest.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph C, second sentence; physical page 68.

distractors.B: Insights are a result of analysis, not the reason tales survive.
distractors.C: Global variation characterises plot forms, not the insights.
distractors.D: The passage compares methods; it does not claim transforming animals.
distractors.E: Oral origin characterises the collected stories.
distractors.F: The biological method supplies an evidence-based test, the opposite of lacking factual basis.

synonymSubstitutions: insights into the development ↔ discover how they have evolved
methods used in biological research ↔ the same approach / phylogenetic analysis

questions.prompt: All the fairy tales analysed by Tehrani
questions.evidence: Checking for variants of these two tales and similar stories from Africa, East Asia and other regions, he ended up with 58 stories recorded from oral traditions.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph D, second sentence; physical page 68.

distractors.A: Biological methods were used to analyse the tales, not to provide the tales themselves.
distractors.B: Not all stories are said to survive for one common reason.
distractors.C: The tales come from several regions, but the sentence asks for a property shared by all 58: oral tradition.
distractors.F: The tales are recorded traditions; they are not theories developed without facts.

synonymSubstitutions: all the fairy tales analysed ↔ 58 stories
were originally spoken ↔ recorded from oral traditions

questions.prompt: Tehrani used techniques from evolutionary biology to find out if 32 __________ existed among 58 stories from around the world.
questions.evidence: Once his phylogenetic analysis had established that they were indeed related, he used the same methods to explore how they have developed and altered over time.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph D, third sentence; physical page 68.

distractors.A: The analysis compared whole stories, not whether an ending existed.
distractors.B: Events occur within the stories; the first research step tested relationships between stories.
distractors.C: A warning is a possible story element, not a relationship among 58 stories.
distractors.E: The stories were recorded, but the analysis tested relatedness, not the existence of records.
distractors.F: Variants were gathered, but the grammatical and evidential target is relationships.
distractors.G: Horror was later found to aid survival, not the initial relationship tested.
distractors.H: People do not denote relations between stories.
distractors.I: Every tale has a plot; the analysis tested links among versions.

synonymSubstitutions: links existed ↔ they were indeed related
techniques from evolutionary biology ↔ phylogenetic analysis

questions.prompt: He also wanted to know which aspects of the stories had fewest 33 __________, as he believed these aspects would be the most important ones.
questions.evidence: First he tested some assumptions about which aspects of the story alter least as it evolves, indicating their importance.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph E, first sentence; physical page 68.

distractors.A: ‘Fewest ending’ is ungrammatical and the research concerns aspects, not number of endings.
distractors.B: Events are a type of aspect later compared; they are not what aspects ‘had fewest’.
distractors.C: Warnings are one category, not the changes counted.
distractors.D: Links were established among stories, not counted within aspects.
distractors.E: Records describe the corpus, not degrees of change.
distractors.G: Horror is a retained feature, not a countable change here.
distractors.H: People are characters, not the changes an aspect has.
distractors.I: Plot is an aspect, not the variation that aspects undergo.

synonymSubstitutions: had fewest variations ↔ alter least
most important ↔ indicating their importance

questions.prompt: Contrary to other beliefs, he found that some 34 __________ that were included in a story tended to change over time, and that the middle of a story seemed no more important than the other parts.
questions.evidence: However, Tehrani found no significant difference in the rate of evolution of incidents compared with that of characters.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph F, first sentence; physical page 69.

distractors.A: The next clause compares the middle with the beginning and ending; ‘ending’ is not the changing items intended here.
distractors.C: Warnings are discussed in the following part of the summary.
distractors.D: Links connect story versions; they are not incidents included in a story.
distractors.E: Records are external documentation, not story content.
distractors.F: Variations are changes, but the blank needs the story elements that change: events.
distractors.G: Horror is the best-preserved aspect, not the changing story items here.
distractors.H: Characters/people also evolve, but the wording maps specifically to incidents/events and the option is ‘events’.
distractors.I: Plot is singular and too broad; the passage explicitly refers to incidents/events.

synonymSubstitutions: events ↔ incidents
tended to change over time ↔ rate of evolution

questions.prompt: He was also surprised that parts of a story which seemed to provide some sort of 35 __________ were unimportant.
questions.evidence: But the really big surprise came when he looked at the cautionary elements of the story.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph G, first sentence; physical page 69. The third sentence says those elements were as flexible as trivial details.

distractors.A: An ending is a structural part, not something a story provides.
distractors.B: A story contains events; it does not ‘provide’ events in the intended survival-lesson sense.
distractors.D: The analysis establishes links between stories, not a message provided by a story.
distractors.E: A story may be recorded, but it does not provide records as a cautionary lesson.
distractors.F: Variations are changes between versions, not a lesson provided.
distractors.G: Horror was the important survival factor, not an unimportant cautionary function.
distractors.H: People are characters, not something provided as a lesson.
distractors.I: Plot is the story structure, not the cautionary information it seems to provide.

synonymSubstitutions: warning ↔ cautionary elements
were unimportant ↔ just as flexible as seemingly trivial details

questions.prompt: The aspect that he found most important in a story’s survival was 36 __________.
questions.evidence: The answer, it would appear, is fear – blood-thirsty and gruesome aspects of the story, such as the eating of the grandmother by the wolf, turned out to be the best preserved of all.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph H, first sentence; physical page 69.

distractors.A: The ending was no more conserved than the middle or beginning.
distractors.B: Events showed no special conservation compared with characters.
distractors.C: Warnings/cautionary elements were flexible and therefore unimportant to survival.
distractors.D: Links were a prerequisite for comparison, not the feature that kept stories alive.
distractors.E: Recording preserves data but is not the story aspect found most important.
distractors.F: Variation is the opposite of preservation.
distractors.H: Characters/people evolved as readily as incidents.
distractors.I: The plot as a whole was not singled out; gruesome fear-producing details were.

synonymSubstitutions: horror ↔ fear / blood-thirsty and gruesome aspects
most important in survival ↔ best preserved of all

questions.prompt: What method did Jamie Tehrani use to test his ideas about fairy tales?

options.A: He compared oral and written forms of the same stories.
options.B: He looked at many different forms of the same basic story.
options.C: He looked at unrelated stories from many different countries.
options.D: He contrasted the development of fairy tales with that of living creatures.

questions.evidence: Checking for variants of these two tales and similar stories from Africa, East Asia and other regions, he ended up with 58 stories recorded from oral traditions.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph D, second sentence; physical page 68.

distractors.A: All 58 were recorded from oral traditions; no oral-versus-written comparison is described.
distractors.C: The phylogenetic analysis established that the stories were related, not unrelated.
distractors.D: He borrowed a biological method; he did not contrast the development of tales with organisms.

synonymSubstitutions: many different forms ↔ variants ... and similar stories
the same basic story ↔ these two tales / related versions

questions.prompt: When discussing Tehrani’s views, Jack Zipes suggests that

options.A: Tehrani ignores key changes in the role of women.
options.B: stories which are too horrific are not always taken seriously.
options.C: Tehrani overemphasises the importance of violence in stories.
options.D: features of stories only survive if they have a deeper significance.

questions.evidence: ‘Even if they’re gruesome, they won’t stick unless they matter,’ he says.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph I, second sentence; physical page 69.

distractors.A: Zipes cites women as victims as a perennial theme, not changes in women’s role that Tehrani ignored.
distractors.B: ‘Won’t stick’ means will not survive unless meaningful, not that horrific stories are dismissed as unserious.
distractors.C: Although Zipes is unconvinced, his stated objection is the need for meaningful relevance, not merely that Tehrani stresses violence too much.

synonymSubstitutions: survive ↔ stick
deeper significance ↔ matter
features of stories ↔ gruesome details / perennial theme

questions.prompt: Why does Tehrani refer to Chinese and Japanese fairy tales?

options.A: to indicate that Jack Zipes’ theory is incorrect
options.B: to suggest that crime is a global problem
options.C: to imply that all fairy tales have a similar meaning
options.D: to add more evidence for Jack Zipes’ ideas

questions.evidence: But Tehrani points out that although this is often the case in Western versions, it is not always true elsewhere.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph I, fourth sentence; physical page 69. The next sentence gives Chinese and Japanese counterexamples.

distractors.B: The examples concern the gender of villain and victim, not the prevalence of crime.
distractors.C: They demonstrate differences across cultures, the opposite of one similar meaning.
distractors.D: They are counterexamples to Zipes’ women-as-victims explanation, not support for it.

synonymSubstitutions: indicate ... theory is incorrect ↔ points out ... it is not always true elsewhere
Chinese and Japanese fairy tales ↔ The Tiger Grandmother versions

questions.prompt: What does Mathias Clasen believe about fairy tales?

options.A: They are a safe way of learning to deal with fear.
options.B: They are a type of entertainment that some people avoid.
options.C: They reflect the changing values of our society.
options.D: They reduce our ability to deal with real-world problems.

questions.evidence: Clasen believes that scary stories teach us what it feels like to be afraid without having to experience real danger, and so build up resistance to negative emotions.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraph J, third sentence; physical page 69.

distractors.B: Clasen says people seek out frightening entertainment; he does not focus on avoidance.
distractors.C: He says habits and morals change but the things that scare us are constant.
distractors.D: He says scary stories build resistance, which increases rather than reduces coping ability.

synonymSubstitutions: safe way ↔ without having to experience real danger
learning to deal with fear ↔ teach us what it feels like / build up resistance to negative emotions
